advances: The new obstruction is realized by Cartesian powers of one fixed centrally symmetric convex body with one integer coordinate and 128 continuous coordinates. Its unique minimum-original-potential transport exceeds the parity budget by an explicit linear amount, every transport restoring that budget pays an explicit linear increase in expected target potential, and its selected geometric origin nevertheless has the maximum possible depth, exactly half the total mixed-integer volume. A varying-block version has minimum-transport energy per integer coordinate tending to one. The general exchangeable midpoint identity identifies the additional source-correlation cost, with the exact coefficient beta when sampling proportional to the beta power of the fiber volume. Accepted 464815b935df9890 already supplies the independent-within-parity construction, its exact entropy budget, and its conditional splitting formula. Accepted 2d941f050262e936 already implies a stronger unrestricted minimum-selector scalar obstruction; the new product-body mechanism and its exact depth calibration are the distinct contribution here. None of these assertions proves or disproves the locked weak Oertel conjecture.

proof:
First verify the information identity and its normalization. Log-concavity implies positivity at every convex combination of positive sites. Hence every lattice site in \(\operatorname{conv}(D)\) lies in \(D\), proving completeness. In particular, every same-parity pair of positive sites has a midpoint in \(D\). The midpoint is integral, so \(\mathbf J\) takes values in \(D\). Its array has source marginal \(p\). Exchangeability remains valid after conditioning on \(\mathbf J\), and \(\mathbf X+\mathbf Y=2\mathbf J\); therefore
\(\mathbb E[\mathbf X\mid\mathbf J]=\mathbb E[\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf J]=\mathbf J\).
These are exactly the row equations defining \(\mathcal F(p)\).

The function \(-\log w\) on the positive set of the extension is convex. Applying its convexity to a nonzero row with coefficients \(r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}/q_{\mathbf J}\) yields
\(q_{\mathbf J}\phi_{\mathbf J}\le\sum_{\mathbf I}r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}\phi_{\mathbf I}\).
Zero rows contribute zero. Summation proves \(G(r)\ge0\), in fact for every array in \(\mathcal F(p)\).

Since \(\mathbf Y=2\mathbf J-\mathbf X\), the maps between \((\mathbf X,\mathbf Y)\) and \((\mathbf X,\mathbf J)\) are inverse on their support. For fixed \(\mathbf X\), they merely relabel the possible values of the second variable. Thus
\(H(r)=\operatorname{Ent}(\mathbf J\mid\mathbf X)=\operatorname{Ent}(\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf X)\).
The definition of mutual information gives \(\operatorname{MI}(\mathbf X;\mathbf Y)=S(p)-H(r)\), since \(\mathbf Y\) has law \(p\). Direct expansion of the canonical definitions gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
G(r)&=S(p)+\sum_{\mathbf J}q_{\mathbf J}\log p_{\mathbf J},\\
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)&=-S(q)-\sum_{\mathbf J}q_{\mathbf J}\log p_{\mathbf J},\\
G(r)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)+I(r)
&=S(p)-H(r)=\operatorname{MI}(\mathbf X;\mathbf Y).
\end{aligned}
\]

Because \(\mathbf R\) is a deterministic function of either source, conditioning on its value partitions each of the source and joint laws into disjoint sets. Expanding entropy over that partition gives the entropy of the parity law plus the average conditional entropy. Applied to \(\operatorname{MI}(\mathbf X;\mathbf Y)\), this gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{MI}(\mathbf X;\mathbf Y)
&=S(\pi)+\operatorname{Ent}(\mathbf X\mid\mathbf R)
+\operatorname{Ent}(\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf R)
-\operatorname{Ent}((\mathbf X,\mathbf Y)\mid\mathbf R)\\
&=S(\pi)+\operatorname{MI}(\mathbf X;\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf R).
\end{aligned}
\]

This proves the general correlation-cost identity. Mutual information and conditional mutual information are nonnegative, because they are relative entropies or averages of relative entropies. For completeness, \(\log t\le t-1\) implies \(\sum_{u_x>0}u_x\log(u_x/v_x)\ge1-\sum_{u_x>0}v_x\ge0\) for probability laws with \(v_x>0\) on the positive support of \(u\). This also proves \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)\ge0\) and \(I(r)\ge0\). Comparing \(\pi\) with the uniform law on \(2^n\) classes gives \(S(\pi)\le n\log2\).

The archived independent-within-parity array is exactly the array of accepted `464815b935df9890`, under the aliases stated above. That fact gives its full construction and the identities \(G+I+D_{\mathrm{KL}}=S(\pi)\) and \(H(r)=S(p)-S(\pi)\). We use those accepted conclusions to know that the budget-feasible set is nonempty. The new general identity quantifies the extra cost when conditional independence is removed; it does not reprove or promote the already accepted special-case construction.

For the changed source law, put \(Z_\beta=\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}e^{-\beta\phi_{\mathbf I}}\). The definition of \(\phi\) gives \(p^{(\beta)}_{\mathbf I}=e^{-\beta\phi_{\mathbf I}}/Z_\beta\) and \(\phi^{(\beta)}=\beta\phi\). Since \(\beta>0\), the beta power of the original extension is again log-concave and has the same positive support. The preceding midpoint feasibility proof therefore applies. Direct expansion now yields

\[
\begin{aligned}
S(p^{(\beta)})&=\beta\sum_{\mathbf I}p^{(\beta)}_{\mathbf I}\phi_{\mathbf I}+\log Z_\beta,\\
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{(\beta)}\|p^{(\beta)})
&=\beta\sum_{\mathbf J}q^{(\beta)}_{\mathbf J}\phi_{\mathbf J}
+\log Z_\beta-S(q^{(\beta)}),\\
\beta G(r^{(\beta)})+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{(\beta)}\|p^{(\beta)})
&=S(p^{(\beta)})-S(q^{(\beta)}).
\end{aligned}
\]

The same invertibility of the midpoint map gives
\(I(r^{(\beta)})=S(q^{(\beta)})-S(p^{(\beta)})+\operatorname{MI}(\mathbf X;\mathbf Y)\).
Adding proves the claimed identity with exactly \(\beta G\). The parity decomposition is unchanged. Applying accepted `464815b935df9890` to the complete table \(w^\beta\) gives its independent-within-parity instance; its canonical energy is \(\beta\) times the original-\(\phi\) energy used here. An inequality established under \(p\) cannot simply be transferred to \(p^{(2)}\), because its source probabilities and expected original potential both change. No such transfer is used.

We next verify the body family, including every fiber. More generally, fix \(a>0\), integers \(L,m\ge1\), and \(aL<m\). Both \(|x|\) and \(2\|\mathbf y\|_\infty+(a/m)|x|\) are convex, so the two constraints defining \(B_{a,L,m}\) define a convex set. It is closed and bounded: \(|x|\le L\) and \(\|\mathbf y\|_\infty\le1/2\). Its origin satisfies the two inequalities strictly, proving nonempty interior. Both constraints are invariant under \((x,\mathbf y)\mapsto(-x,-\mathbf y)\). Thus it is a full-dimensional centrally symmetric convex body.

At a real \(x\in[-L,L]\), its fiber is exactly the cube
\([-(1-a|x|/m)/2,(1-a|x|/m)/2]^m\).
Its side length is positive because \(aL<m\). For \(|x|>L\), the fiber is empty. Therefore its entire integer fiber table is \((1-a|i|/m)^m\) on \(\{-L,\ldots,L\}\), with zero values at every other integer. The grouped \(n\)-fold Cartesian product has integer coordinates \((x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), \(mn\) continuous coordinates, and fibers equal to products of the stated cubes. Their volumes multiply. This proves the full table and total-volume formulas, including the fixed case \(a=\log2,L=4,m=128\), for which \(aL<m\).

These tables satisfy the extension hypothesis directly. On \([-L,L]\), \(1-a|x|/m\) is positive and concave, so its logarithm is concave: concavity of the first function followed by monotonicity and concavity of the logarithm proves the assertion. Consequently \((1-a|x|/m)^m\) is log-concave there. Its zero extension is globally log-concave, since a pair with an endpoint outside the interval has zero required lower bound for every interpolation parameter strictly between zero and one. Taking products proves the corresponding assertion in \(n\) integer-coordinate variables. The support is the complete lattice box. The central weight is one and all other weights are strictly smaller; hence \(\phi\ge0\) and \(\phi_{\mathbf I}=0\) holds only at \(\mathbf I=\mathbf0\). Taking logarithms proves the displayed separated potential formula.

Each one-coordinate distribution is even, so its mean is zero and the product source law has mean \(\mathbf0\). Thus the constant target \(\mathbf J=\mathbf0\) is feasible, and its expected target potential is zero. Every feasible array has nonnegative expected target potential. If that expectation equals zero, every noncentral target has zero row mass because its potential is strictly positive. Nonnegativity makes all entries in those rows zero; the column equations then force \(r_{\mathbf0,\mathbf I}=p_{\mathbf I}\). This proves uniqueness of the minimizer over the entire \(\mathcal F(p)\), without any condition on target-support compression.

The target law is a point mass, so \(S(q^0)=0\). In its sole nonzero row, \(r^0_{\mathbf0,\mathbf I}/p_{\mathbf I}=1\), proving \(H(r^0)=0\) and hence \(I(r^0)=0\). Independence of the product source coordinates and additivity of \(\phi\) give \(G(r^0)=\mathbb E_p[\phi]=n\ell(a,L,m)\). This specializes to the displayed value \(n\ell\).

To prove the explicit fixed-block lower bound, the identity
\(-\log(1-t)-t=\int_0^t u/(1-u)\,du\) gives, for \(0\le t<1\),
\(t\le-\log(1-t)\le t+t^2/(2(1-t))\).
With \(a=\log2\), \(m=128\), and \(1\le i\le4\), this implies

\[
ai\le v_i\le ai+\frac{a^2i^2}{2(m-ai)}
\le ai+\varepsilon_m,\qquad
\varepsilon_m=\frac{8a^2}{m-4a}<\frac2{31}.
\]

The last strict inequality follows from \(0<a<1\): its numerator is less than eight and its denominator is greater than 124. Since \(b_i=e^{-v_i}\) and \(e^{-ai}=2^{-i}\), this gives \(e^{-\varepsilon_m}2^{-i}\le b_i\le2^{-i}\). The finite sums are \(\sum_{i=1}^4 2^{-i}=15/16\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^4i2^{-i}=13/8\). Hence

\[
\begin{aligned}
1+2\sum_{i=1}^4 b_i&\le\frac{23}{8},\\
2\sum_{i=1}^4 b_i v_i&\ge\frac{13a}{4}e^{-\varepsilon_m},\\
\ell&\ge\frac{26}{23}a e^{-\varepsilon_m}
\ge\frac{26}{23}a(1-\varepsilon_m)
>\frac{26}{23}a\frac{29}{31}
=\frac{754}{713}\log2.
\end{aligned}
\]

Here \(e^{-t}\ge1-t\), for example by convexity of the exponential, supplies the middle inequality. This is an exact analytic bound. It proves the claimed strict linear budget excess.

For any feasible \(r\) in this fixed family, the original source marginal stays \(p\), and thus
\(\sum_{\mathbf J}q_{\mathbf J}\phi_{\mathbf J}=n\ell-G(r)\).
The assumed budget gives \(G(r)\le n\log2+K-I(r)\), so

\[
\sum_{\mathbf J}q_{\mathbf J}\phi_{\mathbf J}
\ge n(\ell-\log2)-K+I(r)
>\frac{41}{713}\,n\log2-K,
\]

using \(I(r)\ge0\). The minimum is zero, so this is the asserted cost of recovery. For any fixed real \(K\), taking \(n\) sufficiently large violates the budget at \(r^0\). More generally, if a second fixed constant \(A\ge0\) bounds the allowed increase in expected target potential, the displayed inequality excludes every such budget-feasible array once \((41/713)n\log2-K>A\). The already accepted parity array supplies budget-feasible arrays when \(K\ge0\), so this separation is nonvacuous.

For the varying-block asymptotic, fix \(a>0\) and \(L\). For each of the finitely many integers \(1\le i\le L\), the logarithm bounds above show \(-m\log(1-ai/m)\to ai\) and \((1-ai/m)^m\to e^{-ai}\) as integers \(m\to\infty\). The denominator of \(\ell(a,L,m)\) is at least one, so termwise convergence in these finite sums gives

\[
\lim_{m\to\infty}\ell(a,L,m)
=\frac{2a\sum_{i=1}^L i e^{-ai}}{1+2\sum_{i=1}^L e^{-ai}}.
\]

For fixed \(a>0\), both infinite series converge. Writing \(t=e^{-a}\in(0,1)\), the geometric-series formulas \(\sum_{i\ge1}t^i=t/(1-t)\) and \(\sum_{i\ge1}it^i=t/(1-t)^2\) yield

\[
\lim_{L\to\infty}\lim_{m\to\infty}\ell(a,L,m)
=\frac{2at/(1-t)^2}{(1+t)/(1-t)}
=\frac{2at}{1-t^2}=\frac a{\sinh a}.
\]

Finally \(\sinh a/a\to1\) as \(a\downarrow0\), giving the stated iterated limit. To make its quantifiers explicit, given \(\varepsilon>0\), first choose \(a>0\) with \(|a/\sinh a-1|<\varepsilon/3\). Then choose a finite integer \(L\) so that the preceding finite-sum ratio differs from \(a/\sinh a\) by less than \(\varepsilon/3\). Finally choose an integer \(m>aL\) so that \(\ell(a,L,m)\) differs from that finite-sum ratio by less than \(\varepsilon/3\). These choices depend only on \(\varepsilon\). They give \(|\ell(a,L,m)-1|<\varepsilon\), and all the earlier body, uniqueness, and energy arguments apply for every \(n\). Choosing such blocks along any sequence \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) proves the claimed limiting excess as well as the lower bound.

We verify actual depth for both families independently of any scalar certificate. Let \(\mu\) be the mixed-integer measure restricted to \(C_n\), namely the sum of \(mn\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure over its finitely many integer fibers. Then \(\mu(C_n)=W\), and central inversion preserves \(\mu\): it pairs the fiber at \(\mathbf I\) with its congruent reflected fiber at \(-\mathbf I\). If a closed halfspace \(\mathcal K\) contains the origin, then \(\mathcal K\cup(-\mathcal K)\) contains the whole ambient space. Therefore \(2\mu(\mathcal K)=\mu(\mathcal K)+\mu(-\mathcal K)\ge W\), proving depth at least \(W/2\) at the origin.

Choose one continuous coordinate, for example the first coordinate of the first block's \(\mathbf y\). In every positive fiber it ranges over a centered interval as one factor of a full-dimensional box. Its zero hyperplane has zero \(mn\)-dimensional fiber measure, and its nonnegative and nonpositive halfspaces each have half the fiber volume. Summing shows that either halfspace has mixed volume exactly \(W/2\). This proves \(h_{S_{C_n}}(\mathbf0)=W/2\).

At any other point \(\mathbf z\in S_{C_n}\), let \(t\) be that same continuous coordinate of \(\mathbf z\). If \(t\ge0\), the halfspace where the coordinate is at least \(t\) contains \(\mathbf z\) and is contained in the nonnegative halfspace. If \(t<0\), use instead the halfspace where the coordinate is at most \(t\), contained in the nonpositive halfspace. In either case its mixed volume is at most \(W/2\). Thus every point has depth at most \(W/2\), and the origin attains that value. Since \(W>0\), these bodies satisfy the locked weak Oertel bound for every permitted \(c_0<1/e\); they supply an obstruction only to the specified scalar selector argument.

For the antithetic realization, the product source law is invariant under \(\mathbf X\mapsto-\mathbf X\). Hence \((\mathbf X,-\mathbf X)\) is exchangeable, and its sources have the same parity. Its midpoint is identically zero, giving exactly \(r^0\). The second source is a deterministic invertible function of the first, so \(\operatorname{Ent}(\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf X)=0\) and \(\operatorname{MI}(\mathbf X;\mathbf Y)=S(p)\). Conditionally on their shared parity the same determinism holds, and \(\operatorname{Ent}(\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf R)=S(p)-S(\pi)\), giving \(\operatorname{MI}(\mathbf X;\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf R)=S(p)-S(\pi)\). Equivalently, the general identity at this array reads \(G(r^0)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\delta_{\mathbf0}\|p)=S(p)\). In contrast, the comparison identities \(H(r)=S(p)-S(\pi)\) and \(G+I+D_{\mathrm{KL}}=S(\pi)\) for the conditionally independent array are exactly the accepted conclusions of `464815b935df9890`. This accounts for the selector's zero target-label splitting and the extra source-pair correlation without requiring any unproved relation to geometric depth.

Finally, accepted `2d941f050262e936` supplies complete simplex tables with mean zero, unique maximum at zero, and

\[
G(r^0)=\frac{n}{n+1}\log\frac{\binom{2n+1}{n}-1}{n},\qquad
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{G(r^0)}{n\log2}=2.
\]

Although that fact states its rigidity conclusion using an additional target-support condition, its tabulated weights and mean also give the unrestricted minimum-potential conclusion directly: the zero target is feasible, its expected potential is zero, every other lattice site's potential is positive, and zero expected potential therefore forces the sole row at zero by the same nonnegativity and column-sum argument used above. Thus the earlier fact already yields a stronger unrestricted scalar-budget obstruction at the unique minimum-potential array. Its generally nonsymmetric simplex body and depth calibration are different from the centrally symmetric fixed-block product bodies proved here. No stronger unrestricted obstruction, no bound for a differently weighted second-moment selector, and no implication from scalar-budget failure to small actual depth are inferred.
statement:
All logarithms are natural. Let \(n\ge1\), and let \(w=(w_{\mathbf I})_{\mathbf I\in\mathbb Z^n}\) be a nonnegative, nonzero, finitely supported table admitting a finite-valued globally log-concave extension agreeing with all its lattice values, including zeros. Put \(D=\{\mathbf I:w_{\mathbf I}>0\}\), \(W=\sum_Dw_{\mathbf I}\), \(p_{\mathbf I}=w_{\mathbf I}/W\), \(p_{\max}=\max_Dp_{\mathbf I}\), and \(\phi_{\mathbf I}=\log(p_{\max}/p_{\mathbf I})\) on \(D\). These hypotheses imply \(D=\operatorname{conv}(D)\cap\mathbb Z^n\). Both indices of an array range over \(D\). Use the canonical definitions

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal F(p)&=\left\{r\ge0:
\sum_{\mathbf J}r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}=p_{\mathbf I}\ (\mathbf I\in D),\quad
\sum_{\mathbf I}r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}(\mathbf I-\mathbf J)=\mathbf0\ (\mathbf J\in D)\right\},\\
q_{\mathbf J}&=\sum_{\mathbf I}r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I},\qquad
S(v)=-\sum_xv_x\log v_x,\\
H(r)&=-\sum_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}
\log\frac{r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}}{p_{\mathbf I}},\qquad
I(r)=S(q)-H(r),\\
G(r)&=\sum_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}
(\phi_{\mathbf I}-\phi_{\mathbf J}),\qquad
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)=\sum_{\mathbf J:q_{\mathbf J}>0}q_{\mathbf J}\log\frac{q_{\mathbf J}}{p_{\mathbf J}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Here \(S\) denotes Shannon entropy, and \(H(r)\) denotes conditional assignment entropy. All zero summands are interpreted by continuity. For random variables, write \(\operatorname{Ent}(\cdot\mid\cdot)\) for conditional Shannon entropy, \(\operatorname{MI}(\cdot;\cdot)\) for mutual information, and \(\operatorname{MI}(\cdot;\cdot\mid\cdot)\) for conditional mutual information. Thus \(I(r)=\operatorname{MI}(\mathbf X;\mathbf J)\) when \((\mathbf J,\mathbf X)\) has law \(r\). The archived source's \(V,\mathcal E,\gamma\) are respectively the present \(\phi,G,r\); its Shannon-entropy notation \(H\) is the present \(S\), not the canonical \(H(r)\). Its parity law \(\alpha\) is the present \(\pi\).

Suppose \((\mathbf X,\mathbf Y)\) is any exchangeable pair with both marginals \(p\) and with \(\mathbf X\equiv\mathbf Y\pmod2\) almost surely. Let \(\mathbf J=(\mathbf X+\mathbf Y)/2\), let \(r\) be the law of \((\mathbf J,\mathbf X)\), and let \(\mathbf R=\mathbf X\bmod2=\mathbf Y\bmod2\) have law \(\pi\). Then \(r\in\mathcal F(p)\), \(G(r)\ge0\), and

\[
G(r)+I(r)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)
=\operatorname{MI}(\mathbf X;\mathbf Y)
=S(\pi)+\operatorname{MI}(\mathbf X;\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf R).
\]

The conditional-independent case, including its explicit array, the equality \(G+I+D_{\mathrm{KL}}=S(\pi)\le n\log2\), and \(H(r)=S(p)-S(\pi)\), is invoked from accepted fact `464815b935df9890`; it is not a new assertion of this packet.

For every real \(\beta>0\), set \(p^{(\beta)}_{\mathbf I}=w_{\mathbf I}^{\beta}/\sum_Dw_{\mathbf K}^{\beta}\). For an exchangeable same-parity pair with this changed marginal, write \(r^{(\beta)}\), \(q^{(\beta)}\), and \(\pi^{(\beta)}\) for the corresponding array, target law, and parity law. Define \(\mathcal F(p^{(\beta)})\), \(H(r^{(\beta)})\), and \(I(r^{(\beta)})\) by replacing \(p\) by \(p^{(\beta)}\) in the definitions above. Retain the original \(\phi\) in \(G(r^{(\beta)})\). The canonical potential associated with the changed source law is \(\phi^{(\beta)}=\beta\phi\), so its potential drop is \(\beta G(r^{(\beta)})\). Then

\[
\beta G(r^{(\beta)})+I(r^{(\beta)})
+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{(\beta)}\|p^{(\beta)})
=\operatorname{MI}(\mathbf X;\mathbf Y)
=S(\pi^{(\beta)})+\operatorname{MI}(\mathbf X;\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf R).
\]

In particular, the independent-within-parity construction for \(p^{(\beta)}\) has right-hand side \(S(\pi^{(\beta)})\le n\log2\). At \(\beta=2\) the energy coefficient is exactly two. The original-law selector obstruction below makes no assertion about the weaker budget \(G+I\le n\log2+K\) under the changed law \(p^{(2)}\).

For the explicit product family, fix \(a=\log2\), \(m=128\), and define

\[
\begin{aligned}
B&=\left\{(x,\mathbf y)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^m:
|x|\le4,\quad 2\|\mathbf y\|_\infty+\frac a m|x|\le1\right\},\\
C_n&=B^n\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^{128n},\qquad
b_i=\left(1-\frac{a|i|}{m}\right)^m\quad(-4\le i\le4),\\
v_i&=-m\log\left(1-\frac{a|i|}{m}\right),\qquad
\ell=\frac{2\sum_{i=1}^4b_i v_i}{1+2\sum_{i=1}^4b_i}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For every \(n\ge1\), \(C_n\) is a full-dimensional centrally symmetric convex body with continuous dimension \(d=128n\). Its entire integer fiber-volume table is

\[
\begin{aligned}
D&=\{-4,-3,\ldots,4\}^n,\qquad
w_{\mathbf I}=\prod_{k=1}^n b_{I_k}\quad(\mathbf I\in D),\qquad
w_{\mathbf I}=0\quad(\mathbf I\notin D),\\
W&=\left(1+2\sum_{i=1}^4b_i\right)^n,\qquad
\phi_{\mathbf I}=\sum_{k=1}^n v_{I_k}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Use its original source law \(p=w/W\). There is exactly one minimizer \(r^0\in\mathcal F(p)\) of \(\sum_{\mathbf J}q_{\mathbf J}\phi_{\mathbf J}\). It is \(r^0_{\mathbf0,\mathbf I}=p_{\mathbf I}\), with all other entries zero. Its minimum target potential is zero, and

\[
S(q^0)=H(r^0)=I(r^0)=0,\qquad
G(r^0)=n\ell>\frac{754}{713}\,n\log2
=n\log2+\frac{41}{713}\,n\log2.
\]

For every \(K\in\mathbb R\) and every \(r\in\mathcal F(p)\) satisfying \(G(r)+I(r)\le n\log2+K\), one has

\[
\sum_{\mathbf J}q_{\mathbf J}\phi_{\mathbf J}
\ge n(\ell-\log2)-K+I(r)
>\frac{41}{713}\,n\log2-K.
\]

For \(K\ge0\), such budget-feasible arrays exist by accepted `464815b935df9890`. Thus, even in this fixed-block class, no absolute additive budget allowance makes the minimum-potential selector satisfy the scalar budget, and a bounded additive relaxation of its minimum expected target potential does not restore that budget uniformly in \(n\).

The fixed-body result has the following varying-block limit. For \(a>0\), integers \(L,m\ge1\) with \(m>aL\), replace the constraint \(|x|\le4\) in \(B\) by \(|x|\le L\), retaining the constraint \(2\|\mathbf y\|_\infty+(a/m)|x|\le1\), and call the resulting body \(B_{a,L,m}\). Define

\[
\ell(a,L,m)=
\frac{2\sum_{i=1}^L(1-ai/m)^m[-m\log(1-ai/m)]}
{1+2\sum_{i=1}^L(1-ai/m)^m}.
\]

The original-law minimum-potential transport for \(B_{a,L,m}^n\) is again unique, has \(I=0\), and has \(G=n\ell(a,L,m)\). Moreover,

\[
\lim_{a\downarrow0}\lim_{L\to\infty}\lim_{m\to\infty}\ell(a,L,m)=1,
\]

where \(L,m\) run through integers and the inner limit respects \(m>aL\). Consequently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there are finite \(a,L,m\), independent of \(n\), such that this actual-body product family has \(G(r^0)>(1-\varepsilon)n\) for every \(n\ge1\). Its excess per integer coordinate over the original parity budget can tend to \(1-\log2\).

For every fixed or varying block just specified, let \(C_n\) denote its \(n\)-fold product, let \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^{mn}\), and let \(S_{C_n}=C_n\cap\Lambda\). Mixed-integer volume is the sum of \(mn\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure over integer fibers. Define \(h_{S_{C_n}}(\mathbf z)=\inf_{\mathcal K\ni\mathbf z}\mathcal H_{mn}(S_{C_n}\cap\mathcal K)\), where the infimum ranges over closed halfspaces of the ambient space. Then

\[
h_{S_{C_n}}(\mathbf0)
=\max_{\mathbf z\in S_{C_n}}h_{S_{C_n}}(\mathbf z)
=\frac12\mathcal H_{mn}(S_{C_n})=\frac W2.
\]

The minimum array has the antithetic midpoint realization \(\mathbf Y=-\mathbf X\). For that realization \(\operatorname{MI}(\mathbf X;\mathbf Y)=S(p)\) and \(\operatorname{MI}(\mathbf X;\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf R)=S(p)-S(\pi)\), while \(H(r^0)=0\). The general identity therefore accounts exactly for the difference between this selector and the accepted independent-within-parity construction.

The comparison with accepted `2d941f050262e936` is part of the scope of the result: its original-law simplex tables also have mean zero and a unique maximum at zero. Their constant-target arrays are consequently the unique minimum-potential arrays, with energy divided by \(n\log2\) tending to two. Thus an unrestricted minimum-selector scalar counterexample is already available more strongly from that fact. The new conclusions here concern centrally symmetric powers of a fixed block, the exact \(d=128n\) realization and recovery cost, the near-unit product asymptotic, and actual maximum depth \(W/2\).
